title: Urology and Sexually Transmitted Infections

CHAPTER 8

## Urology and Sexually Transmitted Infections

## CONTENT OVERVIEW

- Urinary tract infections
- Urologic diagnostics
- Acute pyelonephritis
- Hematuria
- Nephrolithiasis
- Chronic kidney disease
- Interstitial cystitis
- Urinary incontinence
- Sexually transmitted infections

## NOTES Urinary Tract Infection

- Bacteria colonize the urethra or periurethral space.
- $ E. coli (most common), Klebsiella pneumoniae, Proteus mirabilis, Staphylococcus saprophyticus
- Risk factors: female sex, recent sexual intercourse, diabetes mellitus, structural/functional urologic abnormalities

## Lower urinary tract

- Dysuria
- Urinary frequency
- Urinary urgency
- Suprapubic pain
- Absence of systemic symptoms

## Uncomplicated vs Complicated UTIs

NEW IDSA Guidelines July 2025

Uncomplicated: infection CONFINED to the bladder in afebrile women or men

Complicated: infection BEYOND the bladder in women or men

- $ Pyelonephritis
- $ Febrile or bacteremic UTI
- $ Catheter-associated (CAUTI)
- $ Systemic symptoms

## UTI Diagnostic Studies

- Urine dipstick: POC test
- Urinalysis: WBCs, protein, nitrites, RBCs, casts, etc.
- Urine microscopy: microscopic visualization of bacteria
- $ Morphology: rods, cocci, etc.
- $ Gram stain
- Urine culture

## Urine Dipstick Interpretation

| Test                | What Is It?                        | What Does It Mean?                                                 |
|---------------------|------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------|
| NitrIte             | Produced by gram-negative bacteria | · Indicates Infection · NitrAtes: "A-ok"                           |
| Leukocytes "Pyuria" | WBCs in the urine                  | · Most reliable indicator of infection                             |
| Leukocyte esterase  | Enzyme produced by WBCs            | · Usually indicates UTI · If absent, consider other differentials. |

<!-- image -->

## Upper urinary tract

- Flank pain
- Costovertebral tenderness
- Systemic symptoms

## QUESTION #1

An asymptomatic patient is found to have bacteriuria on a urine dipstick. Antibiotic therapy is appropriate if the patient:

1. has an indwelling urinary catheter.
2. is immunocompromised.
3. is younger than 7 years.
4. is currently pregnant.

## Empiric Antibiotic Therapy

Acute simple cystitis

| Population   | First-Line Treatment                                                                                              |
|--------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Nonpregnant  | 1. Nitrofurantoin                                                                                                 |
|              | 2. Fosfomycin (off-label for males)                                                                               |
|              | 3. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (if local resistance is <20%)                                                    |
| Pregnant     | Cephalexin, fosfomycin, nitrofurantoin, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (see pregnancy module for more information) |

## UTI: Antibiotic Duration

## Uncomplicated UTI

- Nitrofurantoin: 5 days
- Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole: 3 days
- Fosfomycin: 3 g, single dose

## Complicated UTI

- Treatment is individualized, 7-14 days

## UTI Management

- Prompt treatment to prevent complications!
- Consider phenazopyridine
- $ No more than 2 days!
- $ Discolors urine
- UTI prevention:
- $ Cranberry products may prevent repeat UTI
- $ Adequate hydration
- $ Normal voiding schedule: every 2-4 hours, and after sexual intercourse
- $ Postmenopausal females: topical estrogen

TIP: Hematuria requires further evaluation!!!

<!-- image -->

## QUESTION #2

The following patients are all diagnosed with UTIs and prescribed empiric antibiotics. For which patients should a urine culture be ordered?

1. A 25-year-old female with mild suprapubic pain
2. A 60-year-old male who has benign prostatic hypertrophy
3. A 40-year-old female who had a UTI one year ago
4. A 50-year-old female with perimenopausal symptoms

## When to Get a Urine Culture?

- High-risk populations
- $ Recurrent or refractory infections
- $ Risk for complications
- $ Urinary catheter use
- $ Complicated UTIs
- $ Suspected multidrug-resistant infection
- $ Diagnosis uncertain
- Positive culture

- $ Midstream catch: >100,000 organisms
- $ Catheterization: >1,000 organisms

<!-- image -->

## QUESTION #3

A female patient with a UTI was started on a 5-day course of trimethoprimsulfamethoxazole, 3 days ago. Based on the C & S report, the NP:

| Antibiotic     | Sensitivity   |
|----------------|---------------|
| Ampicillin     | R             |
| Cefuroxime     | S             |
| Nitrofurantoin | S             |
| TMP-SMX        | R             |
| Ciprofloxacin  | S             |

1. continues TMP-SMX for 2 additional days.
2. continues TMP-SMX for 2 days then prescribe 5 days of nitrofurantoin.
3. discontinues TMP-SMX and prescribe a 2-day course of nitrofurantoin.
4. discontinue TMP-SMX and prescribe a 5-day course of nitrofurantoin.

<!-- image -->

## Acute Pyelonephritis

Infection of the upper urinary tract and renal parenchyma

- History
- $ UTI symptoms
- $ Systemic symptoms
- Fever, chills, malaise
- $ Flank, pelvic, or perineal pain
- Physical exam
- $ CVA, abdominal, suprapubic tenderness
- $ Patient may be ill-appearing
- Diagnostics
- $ Urinalysis: pyuria, bacteriuria, hematuria, mild proteinuria, WBC casts
- $ CBC: leukocytosis

## Pyelonephritis Management

Outpatient management:

- IF clinically stable and can tolerate oral meds
- Urine culture: collect before starting antibiotics!

## First-line:

- Fluoroquinolones
- $ Levofloxacin QD x 5 days
- $ Ciprofloxacin Q12h × 7 days
- Trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole DS q12h × 7-14 days

## Alternatives:

- Consider 1g ceftriaxone IM x1 PLUS
- $ Amoxicillin/clavulanate PO q12h x 14 days OR
- $ Oral 3rd or 4th generation cephalosporins

## QUESTION #4

A patient presents to urgent care with reports of fever and dark urine. A urinalysis is positive for blood, protein, and RBC casts. There are no leukocytes or nitrites. What is the appropriate next step?

1. Arrange for the patient to see a hematologist today.
2. Schedule the patient to see a urologist next week.
3. Treat the patient with ciprofloxacin for a complicated UTI.
4. Refer the patient to the ED for an urgent nephrology consult.

<!-- image -->

## NOTES

## NOTES Urine Casts

Microscopic particles made by the kidney

| Cast Type   | Significance                                                                                                                          |
|-------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Hyaline     | Most common and nonspecific; low urine flow, dehydration, vigorous exercise                                                           |
| Crystals    | No clinical significance                                                                                                              |
| RBC         | Always pathologic; consider glomerulonephritis, urinary tract injury                                                                  |
| WBC         | May indicate pyelonephritis (not present in simple UTI) Consider inflammation (nephritis, post-Strep glomerulonephritis) or infection |
| Epithelial  | Acute tubular necrosis (poisoning), hepatitis, something that causes epithelial cell death                                            |

## Hematuria

- Gross hematuria
- $ Visible blood or blood-tinged urine
- Microscopic hematuria
- $ Greater than three RBCs per high-power field on microscopy
- $ Positive blood on dipstick

© Pepermpron/Shutterstock

<!-- image -->

85% of patients with bladder cancer presents with hematuria.

## Hematuria: Evaluation

- Urinary tract
- $ Malignancy
- Kidney, bladder
- $ Infection
- $ Renal calculi
- $ Glomerular disease (AKI)
- $ Hydronephrosis
- $ Polycystic kidneys
- $ Trauma
- $ Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH)

## Risk Factors for Urinary Malignancy

- Age >40 years
- Males > females
- Smoking history
- Occupational exposure
- Alcohol use (excessive)
- Chronic cystitis
- History of pelvic irradiation
- History of analgesic misuse

Hematuria + age ≥40 + risk factors for malignancy = REFER to Urology!

- Outside urinary tract
- $ Coagulopathy
- $ Medications
- $ Exercise-induced
- Resolves in 72 hours
- $ Contamination (menses)

## QUESTION #5

Which imaging study is considered the gold standard for diagnosing kidney stones?

1. Helical CT scan
2. Ultrasonography
3. KUB radiograph
4. Intravenous pyelogram

<!-- image -->

## Nephrolithiasis

- Diagnosis
- $ Gold standard: helical CT scan
- $ Ultrasound when CT scan is unavailable, pregnancy, or pediatrics
- Indications for inpatient management
- $ Fever or suspected UTI
- $ Nausea, vomiting
- $ Uncontrolled or unyielding pain
- $ Inability to urinate

## Nephrolithiasis: Outpatient Management

<!-- image -->

© pixologicstudio/iStock

## Pain control

- NSAIDs

## Stone passage

- Strain urine to collect stones for analysis
- Alpha blocker (tamsulosin) to facilitate passage of 5-10 mm stones

## Urology referral

- Stone >10 mm
- Failure to pass stone in 4 weeks
- Persistent pain
- Multiple/bilateral renal calculi (greater risk of recurrence)

## Renal Function

| Test     | What Is it?                                            | Tip/Pearls                                                                                      |
|----------|--------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Creatine | By product of muscle metabolism                        | · Affected by many factors · Decreases with age/muscle mass · Normal doesn't always mean normal |
| UACR     | Measures albuminuria, rare in absence of kidney damage | · Screening for early glomerular disease · Monitors CKD progression & response to treatments    |

| Albuminuria Category   | Range (mg/g)   |
|------------------------|----------------|
| A1                     | <30            |
| A2                     | 30-299         |
| A3                     | >300           |

## Estimated Glomerular Filtration Rate

Chronic kidney disease

- eGFR <60 mL/min, and/or
- Evidence of kidney damage (UACR >30 mg/g)
- Changes present for >3 months

| eGFR Result   | Stage of CKD   |
|---------------|----------------|
| ≥90           | 1              |
| 60-89         | 2              |
| 45-59         | 3a             |
| 30-44         | 3b             |
| 15-29         | 4              |
| <15           | 5              |

Abnormal kidney function is treated as acute unless proven otherwise!

## Prescribing in Renal Impairment

Consider baseline renal function; dosage adjustments if low GFR

- Metformin, allopurinol, statins
- ACEs/ARBs, diuretics, antiarrhythmics
- Many antibiotics
- $ Several beta-lactams, levofloxacin, TMP-SMX, clarithromycin, nitrofurantoin
- NSAIDs, tramadol
- Lithium, gabapentin
- H2 blockers, some antihistamines

## QUESTION #6

A young adult female reports chronic bladder pain, urinary urgency, and frequency. Interstitial cystitis is suspected. Which statement about interstitial cystitis is incorrect?

1. Voiding may occur up to 60 times a day.
2. Long-term antibiotic prophylaxis is recommended.
3. Urology consultation is helpful for diagnosis and treatment recommendations.
4. Eliminating bladder irritants may reduce symptoms.

## Interstitial Cystitis

"Bladder pain syndrome"

- Symptoms
- $ Urinary frequency or urgency
- $ Dysuria
- $ Bladder pain
- $ Pelvic pain
- Etiology unknown
- Rule out differentials
- Urology referral
- $ Cystoscopy
- $ Bladder biopsy

## Types of Incontinence

Estimated prevalence: 25-40%

- 40% of females >70 years
- <30% of incontinent females seek care

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

© VectorMine/iStock /Getty Images Plus/Getty Images

<!-- image -->

## Incontinence/OAB: Management

Behavioral management: first-line

- Bladder training
- Fluid management
- $ Minimize fluids after dinner
- $ Take diuretics in afternoon, NOT at night
- Pelvic floor exercises (Kegel, yoga, pelvic tilts)

## Incontinence/OAB: Pharmacotherapy

Urge/mixed incontinence

Anticholinergics first-line:

- Oxybutynin (Ditropan), Tolterodine (Detrol)
- Side effects: dry mouth, dry eyes, gastrointestinal

Alternate anticholinergic drug:

- $ Mirabegron (Myrbetriq): beta-3 agonist
- fewer side effects
- Postmenopausal females: topical estrogen

"Ode to anticholinergics"

Can't S, P, S, S

## SEXUALLY TRANSMITTED INFECTIONS

## WHAT TO KNOW-STIs

- Chlamydia
- Gonorrhea
- Trichomoniasis
- Syphilis
- Herpes simplex virus (HSV)
- Human immunodeficiency Virus (HIV)
- Bacterial vaginosis (BV)
- Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID)
- Sexual assault evaluation

## ASSESSING SEXUAL RISK

- 5Ps of sexual history
- $ Partners
- $ Practices
- $ Protection from STIs
- $ Past history of STIs
- $ Pregnancy intention
- Presenting symptoms
- $ Males vs. females
- Diagnostics
- $ Screening
- $ Diagnosis
- $ Sample (swab, serology)
- Management

CDC's 2021 STI Treatment Guidelines

- High risk
- $ Unprotected sexual intercourse
- $ Multiple sex partners
- $ Sex under the influence
- $ Early sexual initiation
- $ High risk partner

Nonpharmacologic options:

- Biofeedback, nerve stimulation
- Pessaries-pelvic organ prolapse
- Surgery-stress incontinence
- Weight loss-stress incontinence

## QUESTION #7

A 23-year-old female presents with dysuria and vaginal discharge. She reports unprotected sex with two partners in the last 3 months. The urine dipstick shows pyuria, but negative for nitrites or blood. What is the next best step to manage this patient?

1. Treat for a UTI caused by gram-positive organisms.
2. Treat for gonorrhea, chlamydia, and UTI.
3. Repeat urinalysis with a first-morning sample.
4. Perform testing for sexually transmitted infections.

<!-- image -->

TIP: test and treat to minimize complications

## STI Symptoms

Patients are often ASYMPTOMATIC!!!

## Females

- Vaginal discharge
- Dysuria
- Salpingitis
- Abnormal vaginal bleeding
- Pelvic pain

## Bacterial Vaginosis

Sexually associated, NOT sexually transmitted

- Risks
- $ Associated with multiple sex partners, new partners, douching, IUCs
- $ Higher risk for STIs
- Diagnosis: Amsel criteria (3 of 4)
- $ Thin, milklike discharge, coating vaginal walls
- $ Positive whiff amine
- $ Clue cells
- $ Vaginal pH >4.5
- Treatment
- $ Metronidazole 500 mg PO BID × 7 days
- $ Metronidazole gel 0.75% one full applicator (5 g) PV, QD × 5 days
- $ Clindamycin cream 2% one full applicator (5 g) PV QHS at × 7 days

## Males

- Dysuria
- Penile discharge
- Pelvic pain

## Chlamydia

Most frequently reported infectious disease in the United States, rates increasing

- Serious sequelae: PID, ectopic pregnancy, infertility, pelvic pain
- Typically, asymptomatic
- Most common in patients <25 years
- Screening:
- $ Sexually active females <25 yearly
- $ Sexually active females ≥25 years if at increased risk
- $ Pregnant patients

## Chlamydia: Diagnostic Studies

## NAAT most sensitive

- Vaginal
- Cervical
- Rectal
- First-void urine
- Patient or provider collected
- Point-of-care (POC) testing and home tests available
- Optimizes early treatment

## QUESTION #8

What is the first-line treatment for chlamydia?

1. Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM × 1
2. Azithromycin 1 g oral single dose
3. Levofloxacin 500 mg oral × 7 days
4. Doxycycline 100 mg orally BID for 7 days

## Chlamydia Management

## Nonpregnant:

- First line: doxycycline 100 mg orally BID × 7 days
- $ Levofloxacin 500 mg orally once daily × 7 days
- $ Azithromycin 1 g orally single dose

## Pregnant:

- First line: azithromycin 1 g orally single dose
- $ Amoxicillin 500 mg TID × 7 days

## Retest:

- $ ALL patients 3 months after antibiotics
- $ Pregnant patients: 1 month, 3 months, and 3rd trimester

Persistent symptoms 1 month after treatment, consider reinfection

<!-- image -->

## NOTES

## NOTES Gonorrhea

Produces a purulent inflammation of mucous membranes Higher risk

- Men who have sex with men (MSM)
- IV drug use
- Underdiagnosed in the United States
- Uncommon among "monogamous heterosexual populations"

## QUESTION #9

According to the 2021 CDC guidelines for STI treatment, what is the recommended initial screening test for gonorrhea in an asymptomatic patient?

1. Urine culture
2. Nucleic acid amplification test
3. Gram stain
4. Serologic tests

## Gonorrhea Diagnostic Studies

- Nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs)
- $ Urine sample or site-specific swab
- Culture swab site of infection
- $ Vaginal, endocervical, urethral, rectal, oropharyngeal, conjunctival
- Test of cure not indicated in uncomplicated urogenital/rectal gonorrhea

## Gonorrhea Management

Ceftriaxone IM

- 500 mg once if <330 lb (150 kg)
- 1 g once if >330 lb

Cotreatment for chlamydia is not recommended

- If chlamydia cannot be ruled out:
- $ Give doxycycline 100 mg PO BID × 7 days

<!-- image -->

© Henadzi Pechan/iStock/Getty Images Plus/Getty Images

<!-- image -->

## Trichomoniasis

Infects vagina, Skene ducts, and lower genitourinary tract in females and lower genitourinary tract in males

Joshua Lanclos / APEA

<!-- image -->

Parasite: protozoan T. vaginalis Flagellated and motile

## Trichomoniasis: Diagnostic Studies

Nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs)

- Swab for vaginal or urethral discharge

Microscopy and vaginal pH

- Wet prep (60-70% sensitive)
- Visualization of trichomonads
- Vaginal pH >4.6

Pap: unreliable (false positives)

## Trichomoniasis Management

Female, pregnant patients, & females with HIV

- Metronidazole 500 mg PO BID × 7 days
- Alternative (nonpregnant, no HIV):
- $ Tinidazole (single dose) for those who cannot complete the 7-day course
- Alternative (pregnancy):
- $ Metronidazole 2 g orally in a single dose

## Male

- Metronidazole 2 g orally in a single dose
- $ Alternative: Single-dose tinidazole

Retest 3 months [NAAT] after completion

<!-- image -->

## QUESTION #10

A female patient who is diagnosed with early pelvic inflammatory disease is being treated. Which of the following is true of PID?

1. PID presents with obvious symptoms that make diagnosis straightforward.
2. Only severe PID is associated with damage to the genitourinary tract.
3. Infertility and adverse perinatal outcomes are not associated with PID.
4. PID may present with dyspareunia, menorrhagia, or abnormal uterine bleeding.

## PID: Diagnostic Criteria

<!-- image -->

## Minimum criteria

- Lower abdominal pain and/or tenderness
- Cervical motion tenderness, with or without mucous
- Adnexal tenderness

## Additional criteria (one should be present)

- Fever >100.4°F (38°C)
- Wet mount: WBCs >10 per HPF (predictive)
- Pelvic mass on exam
- ESR >15 mm/hour
- Positive endocervical N. gonorrhoeae or C. trachomatis

## Outpatient PID Treatment

<!-- image -->

- Do NOT remove IUD unless no improvement within 48 to 72 hours. · Do NOT remove IUD unless no improvement within 48 to 72 hours.
- Consider inpatient treatment if not responding to regimens, · Consider inpatient treatment if not responding to regimens, pregnancy, or severe cases.

pregnancy, or severe cases.

<!-- image -->

## Syphilis Screening

- Screen symptomatic patients
- Asymptomatic patients at risk
- $ Pregnant patients
- $ Increased risk
- Sexual partner with syphilis
- MSM
- People who have HIV
- Receiving pre-exposure prophylaxis
- Engaged in high-risk sexual behaviors (e.g., condomless sex with multiple partners, exchange sex for money, etc.)
- History of incarceration or commercial sex work

## Assessment Findings: Primary Syphilis

- Painless chancre at site of inoculation
- Solitary or multiple genital lesions
- Persists for 1-5 weeks
- Heals spontaneously
- Regional lymphadenopathy

<!-- image -->

Highly contagious at this stage, may go unnoticed.

Reprinted with permission from Velho PE, Souza EM, Belda Junior W. Donovanosis. Braz J Infect Dis. 2008;12(6):523.

<!-- image -->

## NOTES

## NOTES Assessment Findings: Secondary Syphilis

- Rash characteristics
- $ Bilaterally symmetrical
- $ Polymorphic, nonpruritic
- $ Soles and palms
- $ Lasts 2-6 weeks
- Spontaneously resolves
- Condyloma lata:
- $ moist, pink, peripheral warty lesions`
- Glans
- Perianal
- Vulval
- Intertriginous areas

## Assessment Findings: Latent Syphilis

Asymptomatic with positive serology

<!-- image -->

## Early: acquired in last 12 months. If in the preceding year,

- documented seroconversion
- sustained (>2 weeks) ≥ fourfold increase in nontreponemal titers (previously treated)
- unequivocal symptoms of primary or secondary syphilis
- sex partner with documented syphilis

Late: asymptomatic, present for >1 year

## Tertiary (Late) Syphilis

Serious complications of late latent syphilis

- Cardiovascular: aortic valve disease, aneurysms
- Neurologic: neurosyphilis, meningitis, encephalitis, dementia
- Integumentary: gummas
- Orthopedic: Charcot joints, osteomyelitis

<!-- image -->

## Types of Syphilis Tests

Nontreponemal

- Rapid plasma reagin (RPR)
- Venereal disease research laboratory (VDRL)
- Toluidine red unheated serum test (TRUST)

## Treponemal

- Immunoassay (TP-EIA)
- Fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption (FTA-ABS)
- T. pallidum particle agglutination assay (TPPA)

## Syphilis Testing: Traditional Approach

<!-- image -->

## Syphilis Treatment

Primary, secondary, & early latent

- First-line: benzathine penicillin G (Bicillin) 2.4 million units IM × 1 (children: 50,000 units/kg IM)
- Sexual partners: prophylaxis indicated for all partners in last 90 days, regardless of test results Tertiary & late latent
- First-line: penicillin G benzathine 2.4 million units IM weekly × 3 weeks
- Sexual partners: serologic testing for syphilis

PCN allergic: desensitization recommended

## Syphilis Test of Cure

Primary, secondary, & early latent

- Nontreponemal titers at 6 and 12 months
- $ More frequently if patient has HIV

Tertiary & late latent

- Nontreponemal titers at 6, 12, and 24 months

A fourfold decrease indicates adequate treatment.

## NOTES

## NOTES HSV-1 vs. HSV-2

- HSV-1 and HSV-2 cause genital herpes
- HSV-2 causes most recurrent genital herpes
- HSV-2 increases risk of HIV twoto three-fold!
- HSV-1 in genital area is not likely to cause recurrent

Ubiquitous exposure to HSV

## Types of HSV Infection

- Primary: no antibodies to HSV-1 or 2
- $ First outbreak
- $ May be mild or severe and prolonged
- Nonprimary: preexisting antibodies to HSV-1 or 2
- $ Recurrent infection: common
- $ Typically, less severe
- $ Asymptomatic viral shedding
- $ More common in HSV-2, first year after primary infection

<!-- image -->

## QUESTION #12

According to the CDC, which of the following is an indication for herpes testing?

1. Five or more sexual partners
2. Current yeast vaginitis
3. HIV-negative status
4. Current genital lesion

## Genital Herpes Testing

<!-- image -->

## Genital lesion

- NAAT (most accurate)
- Culture

## Consider HSV serology IF:

- Genital symptoms that could be related to herpes
- Sexual partner with genital herpes
- Signs of herpes, but confirmation needed

## QUESTION #13

If herpes serology IgG is positive, what should be done?

<!-- image -->

If the patient was exposed to HSV-2 but the serology IgG is negative, repeat the test in 12 weeks.

<!-- image -->

## QUESTION #14

Which of the following patients should be screened for HIV at least once?

1. All patients aged 13-64 years
2. Patients being treated for tuberculosis or hepatitis
3. Patients who have recurrent urinary tract infections
4. More than one sex partner since last HIV test

## HIV: Screening Per CDC

<!-- image -->

Average risk: one-time screening between 13 and 64 years

## High risk: at least annual testing

- MSM
- Anal/vaginal sex with a partner who has HIV
- More than one sex partner since last HIV test
- Sharing needles, syringes, or other drug equipment
- Exchanged sex for drugs or money
- Diagnosed or treated for another STI
- Diagnosed or treated for hepatitis or tuberculosis
- Had sex with any of the above

## NOTES

## NOTES

## QUESTION #15

An asymptomatic patient is screened for HIV infection. What is the preferred initial screening test for HIV?

1. Venereal Disease Research Laboratory (VRDL) IgM and IgG test
2. HIV-1/HIV-2 antibody differentiation immunoassay
3. HIV-1/2 antigen antibody combination immunoassay (ELISA/ELIA)
4. HIV RNA nucleic acid test (NAAT)

<!-- image -->

## QUESTION #16

A patient presents with fever, diarrhea, muscle aches, and swollen cervical lymph nodes. History reveals possible HIV exposure 3 weeks ago. Which of the following tests screens for acute HIV infection?

1. HIV IgM antibodies
2. Antigen/antibody immunoassay (ELISA/EIA)
3. Western blot
4. HIV-1 RNA nucleic acid test (APTIMA)

## HIV Diagnostic Tests

<!-- image -->

## Primary Care Pearls of Adults Infected With HIV

- Never give live or attenuated vaccines!
- HIV is significant risk factor for reactivation of latent TB.
- Pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP) treatment is driven by CD4 count.
- $ TMP-SMX first-line, one dose daily
- Consider referring to infectious disease if not comfortable with treatment.

<!-- image -->

## HIV Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis (PrEP)

Antiretroviral therapy (ART) for HIV prevention Reduces risk of HIV transmission by >99%

- All sexually active patients should be educated about HIV PrEP.
- Identify high-risk patients.

## Eligibility

- High risk for HIV
- Nonreactive HIV antibody/antigen
- No possible exposure to HIV in prior 4 weeks
- No signs/symptoms of acute HIV infection
- Ensure proper workup and recurrent diagnostics if ART is initiated

## PrEP Therapy

|            | Drug                                                           | Considerations                                                                                                      |
|------------|----------------------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Oral       | Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate- emtricitabine (TDF-FTC)/Truvada | Renal impairment/toxicity Bone loss Avoid in patients with eGFR <60 mL/min Event-driven dosing in specific patients |
| Oral       | Tenofovir alafenamide- emtricitabine (TAF-FTC)/Descovy         | Use patients with eGFR 30-60 mL/min or risk for bone loss Avoid in HIV receptive vaginal sex or injection drug use  |
| Injectable | Cabotegravir (monthly × 2 months, then q2 months)/ Apretude    | Patient with eGFR <30 mL/min Patient with risks for or bone disease (i.e., osteoporosis)                            |

90-day supplies with confirmation of negative HIV

is immunocompromised.
is younger than 7 years.
is currently pregnant.

questions.stem: The following patients are all diagnosed with UTIs and prescribed empiric antibiotics. For which patients should a urine culture be ordered?
options: A 25-year-old female with mild suprapubic pain
A 60-year-old male who has benign prostatic hypertrophy
A 40-year-old female who had a UTI one year ago
A 50-year-old female with perimenopausal symptoms When to Get a Urine Culture?

A patient presents to urgent care with reports of fever and dark urine. A urinalysis is positive for blood, protein, and RBC casts. There are no leukocytes or nitrites. What is the appropriate next step?
options: Arrange for the patient to see a hematologist today.
Schedule the patient to see a urologist next week.
Treat the patient with ciprofloxacin for a complicated UTI.
Refer the patient to the ED for an urgent nephrology consult.

questions.stem: Which imaging study is considered the gold standard for diagnosing kidney stones?
options: Helical CT scan
Ultrasonography
KUB radiograph

Intravenous pyelogram Nephrolithiasis - Diagnosis - Gold standard: helical CT scan - Ultrasound when CT scan is unavailable, pregnancy, or pediatrics - Indications for inpatient management - Fever or suspected UTI - Nausea, vomiting - Uncontrolled or unyielding pain - Inability to urinate Nephrolithiasis: Outpatient Management © pixologicstudio/iStock Pain control - NSAIDs Stone passage - Strain urine to collect stones for analysis - Alpha blocker (tamsulosin) to facilitate passage of 5-10 mm stones Urology referral - Stone >10 mm - Failure to pass stone in 4 weeks - Persistent pain - Multiple/bilateral renal calculi (greater risk of recurrence) Renal Function | Test | What Is it? | Tip/Pearls | |----------|--------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------| | Creatine | By product of muscle metabolism | · Affected by many factors · Decreases with age/muscle mass · Normal doesn't always mean normal | | UACR | Measures albuminuria, rare in absence of kidney damage | · Screening for early glomerular disease · Monitors CKD progression & response to treatments | | Albuminuria Category | Range (mg/g) | |------------------------|----------------| | A1 | <30 | | A2 | 30-299 | | A3 | >300 | Estimated Glomerular Filtration Rate Chronic kidney disease - eGFR <60 mL/min, and/or - Evidence of kidney damage (UACR >30 mg/g) - Changes present for >3 months | eGFR Result | Stage of CKD | |---------------|----------------| | ≥90 | 1 | | 60-89 | 2 | | 45-59 | 3a | | 30-44 | 3b | | 15-29 | 4 | | <15 | 5 | Abnormal kidney function is treated as acute unless proven otherwise!

questions.stem: A young adult female reports chronic bladder pain, urinary urgency, and frequency. Interstitial cystitis is suspected. Which statement about interstitial cystitis is incorrect?
options: Voiding may occur up to 60 times a day.
Long-term antibiotic prophylaxis is recommended.
Urology consultation is helpful for diagnosis and treatment recommendations.
Eliminating bladder irritants may reduce symptoms.

questions.stem: A 23-year-old female presents with dysuria and vaginal discharge. She reports unprotected sex with two partners in the last 3 months. The urine dipstick shows pyuria, but negative for nitrites or blood. What is the next best step to manage this patient?
options: Treat for a UTI caused by gram-positive organisms.
Treat for gonorrhea, chlamydia, and UTI.
Repeat urinalysis with a first-morning sample.
Perform testing for sexually transmitted infections.

questions.stem: What is the first-line treatment for chlamydia?
options: Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM × 1
Azithromycin 1 g oral single dose
Levofloxacin 500 mg oral × 7 days

Doxycycline 100 mg orally BID for 7 days Chlamydia Management Nonpregnant: - First line: doxycycline 100 mg orally BID × 7 days - Levofloxacin 500 mg orally once daily × 7 days - Azithromycin 1 g orally single dose Pregnant: - First line: azithromycin 1 g orally single dose - Amoxicillin 500 mg TID × 7 days Retest: - ALL patients 3 months after antibiotics - Pregnant patients: 1 month, 3 months, and 3rd trimester Persistent symptoms 1 month after treatment, consider reinfection NOTES NOTES Gonorrhea Produces a purulent inflammation of mucous membranes Higher risk - Men who have sex with men (MSM) - IV drug use - Underdiagnosed in the United States - Uncommon among "monogamous heterosexual populations" QUESTION #9 According to the 2021 CDC guidelines for STI treatment, what is the recommended initial screening test for gonorrhea in an asymptomatic patient?
Urine culture
Nucleic acid amplification test

questions.stem: A female patient who is diagnosed with early pelvic inflammatory disease is being treated. Which of the following is true of PID?
options: PID presents with obvious symptoms that make diagnosis straightforward.
Only severe PID is associated with damage to the genitourinary tract.
Infertility and adverse perinatal outcomes are not associated with PID.
PID may present with dyspareunia, menorrhagia, or abnormal uterine bleeding.

questions.stem: Which of the following patients should be screened for HIV at least once?
options: All patients aged 13-64 years
Patients being treated for tuberculosis or hepatitis
Patients who have recurrent urinary tract infections

More than one sex partner since last HIV test HIV: Screening Per CDC Average risk: one-time screening between 13 and 64 years High risk: at least annual testing - MSM - Anal/vaginal sex with a partner who has HIV - More than one sex partner since last HIV test - Sharing needles, syringes, or other drug equipment - Exchanged sex for drugs or money - Diagnosed or treated for another STI - Diagnosed or treated for hepatitis or tuberculosis - Had sex with any of the above NOTES NOTES QUESTION #15 An asymptomatic patient is screened for HIV infection. What is the preferred initial screening test for HIV?
Venereal Disease Research Laboratory (VRDL) IgM and IgG test
HIV-1/HIV-2 antibody differentiation immunoassay

questions.stem: A patient presents with fever, diarrhea, muscle aches, and swollen cervical lymph nodes. History reveals possible HIV exposure 3 weeks ago. Which of the following tests screens for acute HIV infection?
options: HIV IgM antibodies
Antigen/antibody immunoassay (ELISA/EIA)
Western blot
HIV-1 RNA nucleic acid test (APTIMA) HIV Diagnostic Tests Primary Care Pearls of Adults Infected With HIV - Never give live or attenuated vaccines!
